idiom_name: Diesel join-table struct with explicit joins
implementation_notes: Diesel's associations are child-to-parent only, and it generates joinable! instances solely for single, non-composite foreign keys - so a many-to-many is declared, not inferred: the link table becomes its own table! struct with the two columns, and queries join the three tables explicitly with an ON clause. Link rows are inserted and deleted as ordinary rows inside a transaction, and loading a collection for many owners is a grouped query (belonging_to plus group_by) rather than a per-owner loop. This is the pattern fully hand-written, which is what most Rust SQL code does.
pitfalls: Inserting the same pair twice fails on the composite primary key (or silently duplicates without one): on_conflict_do_nothing or a prior existence check is required for idempotent linking.
N+1 is easy to write by accident when loading many owners - group rows by owner with group_by and assemble in memory instead of querying per owner.
Diesel's compile-time query types make composite-key joins verbose; adding a third column to the link table changes the table! macro and therefore many query types.

variants.name: SeaORM relation through a junction entity
variants.implementation_notes: SeaORM raises the association to the entity layer: the junction table is declared as an entity holding the two foreign keys, and the many-to-many is expressed by relating the two ends through it, so application code loads a model with find_related and the ORM composes the join. Link rows are written through actor_film::Entity::insert, and the junction entity can carry extra columns, which is the association-entity promotion built into the API. Choose it over Diesel when an async, entity-first ORM is wanted; the join table is still a declared entity, so the association is never invisible.
pitfalls: The junction entity must declare the composite primary key or a unique index on the pair, otherwise repeated inserts duplicate the association.
Calling find_related(...).all(db) once per owner recreates N+1 queries; use find_with_related for a batch or an explicit joined query when loading many owners.
Inserting the link does not create the endpoints - SeaORM writes the row you give it, so ids must exist or the foreign key fails.
